title: Book 8 — Urania, Chapter 118
paragraphs: There is also another story reported, namely that when Xerxes, marching away from Athens, came to Eïon on the Strymon, from that point he did not continue by road but handed his army over to Hydarnes to lead back to the Hellespont, while he himself embarked on a Phoenician ship and set out for Asia. As he sailed, he was caught by a wind from the Strymon, violent and raising great waves; and since he was tossed by the storm worse and worse, the ship being heavily laden (for great numbers of Persians — those who traveled with Xerxes — were on deck), the king, falling into fear, shouted out to ask the pilot whether there was any means of safety for them. The pilot said: “Master, there is none, unless some way can be found to rid ourselves of the excessive number of passengers.” Then it is said that Xerxes, on hearing this, spoke thus: “Persians, now let each one of you show that he has concern for the king; for my safety, it seems, depends on you.” So he spoke, they say, and the Persians made obeisance to him and leapt into the sea; and so the ship, lightened, came safely to Asia. As soon as they had landed Xerxes, it is said, he first presented the pilot with a wreath of gold for having saved the king's life, and then cut off his head, because he had caused the death of many Persians.
